findings.text: One upper bound for base confidential guest identifiers is visible to other files, while the remaining lower and upper bounds for base, extended, and SNP modes together with the encryption mask, identifier count, and allocation and reclaim sets stay file-private.
A dedicated mutex serializes operations that mirror an encryption context from one virtual machine into another.

Checking whether a virtual machine uses confidential guest mode needs no lock when the machine has no remaining users or when the caller runs in vCPU context; otherwise the caller must hold the virtual machine lock, enforced in validation builds.
Three helpers report base, extended, and SNP guest state; each first validates locking as above and then delegates to an unchecked low-level test.
SNP guest state is treated as valid only when extended guest state is also active, with a consistency check guarding any violation.
A tracked memory region links into a per-VM list and records the user range it covers along with its pinned page collection and page count.

Identifier recycling first probes for any reclaimable entry in the requested interval and reports busy when none exists; otherwise it excludes concurrent deactivation, performs a system-wide cache writeback, issues the firmware flush suited to SNP or legacy mode, and then merges the reclaimed set back into the allocatable set.
Firmware deactivation is guarded against cache flush and identifier reuse: recycling holds the guard for writing while unbinding holds it for reading.
A virtual machine counts as mirroring exactly when its stored owner for the encryption context is non-empty.
Debug-swap support and secure timestamping are read from per-VM feature flags; secure timestamping additionally requires SNP guest state.
Resource accounting selects the extended or base confidential-VM resource type from the extended-active flag and charges or releases a single unit.
Allocation searches the requested interval for a free identifier while holding the bitmap guard; when the interval is full it attempts a single recycle and rescans once before reporting exhaustion.

Identifier creation picks the SNP, extended, or base interval from the VM type and extended flag, treats an inverted interval as unsupported, acquires a cgroup reference and charge, and then allocates; allocation failure releases the charge and reference.
Release marks the identifier reclaimable instead of freeing it immediately and clears cached per-CPU references to it, then drops the accounting charge and reference.
Decommission and unbind treat a zero handle as success without firmware interaction; non-zero handles deactivate before decommissioning.
Failures while transitioning a page between private and shared states mark the VM as bugged, record the page as leaked, and return an I/O error.
The bug helper evaluates its condition a single time and moves a VM into the bugged state on its first observed failure.
SNP request support allocates a zeroed request page and a separate firmware response page and initializes its mutex; cleanup frees whichever pages exist and clears both pointers.
Each confidential VM owns a CPU mask recording where it has run; allocation zeroes it and release frees it and clears the reference.

Initialization rejects pre-existing vCPUs, nonzero control flags, unsupported feature bits, and out-of-range protocol versions, defaults extended guests to the newer protocol, requires the newer protocol for SNP, then enables active state, obtains identifier, platform support, CPU mask, and for SNP request buffers, prepares region lists, and inhibits APIC virtualization; each failure unwinds earlier steps.

Legacy initialization derives the guest kind from the command identifier and forces minimal protocol for extended guests, while the newer path requires prior need-init state and an explicit VM type and reads its parameters from userspace; both converge on common initialization.
Binding associates the current VM identifier with a firmware handle through an activation step and propagates firmware errors.
Command issuance through a file descriptor fails as a bad descriptor when the descriptor is empty and otherwise forwards to the external firmware interface.

Launch start requires base guest state, gathers optional peer and session blobs from userspace, starts the firmware context, binds the identifier, and returns the handle to userspace; binding or copy-back failure tears down the new handle and frees the blobs.
Pinning is bounded by total system memory and by the caller memlock limit unless the caller holds the IPC-lock privilege; exceeding either bound fails.
Pinning and unpinning of user memory must run with the VM lock held and maintain a per-VM count of locked pages; partial pin failures release what was pinned.
Cache flushing of pinned pages is skipped on hardware with coherent encryption or when there is nothing to flush; otherwise each page is flushed with rescheduling allowed.
Writeback of guest-tagged caches targets exactly the CPUs recorded as having run the VM and never shrinks that recording.
Encryption uses hardware-adjusted page addresses and groups physically adjacent pages so each firmware update covers one contiguous run with correct intra-page offset.

Data launch update pins the user range for writing, flushes caches, iterates contiguous runs issuing per-run firmware updates, then marks all pages dirty and accessed before unpinning even on failure.

Synchronizing the encrypted save area requires the vCPU mutex and refuses protected guests, active guest debugging, or debug control bits outside the fixed pattern; on success it seeds the separate save area from the current control block and general registers.

Guest kinds are distinguished as default, base, extended, and SNP VM types, and the guest communication protocol uses a defined minimum and maximum with extended guests defaulting to the newer level and SNP requiring at least that level.
